questions.q: Identify the narrative perspective used in "The Tiger King" and quote the first sentence that establishes it.
questions.a: The story uses a first-person narrative perspective ("I have come forward to tell you why he came to be known as Tiger King"). A wrong answer (e.g., "third-person omniscient") reveals the student cannot distinguish the narrator's explicit self-reference ("I") from an invisible narrator, missing how the "I" creates intimacy and irony by pretending to be an insider revealing secrets.

questions.q: Explain how the sentence structure in the opening paragraph — specifically the long list of titles separated by commas — contributes to the story's satirical tone.
questions.a: The cumulative sentence structure piles up grandiose titles ("His Highness Jamedar-General, Khiledar-Major, Sata Vyaghra Samhari, Maharajadhiraja Visva Bhuvana Samrat, Sir Jilani Jung Jung Bahadur, M.A.D., A.C.T.C., or C.R.C.K.") to mock the Maharaja's absurd self-importance; the breathless length mimics bureaucratic pomposity. A wrong answer (e.g., "it shows his greatness") reveals the student reads literally, missing how syntax itself performs satire — the form enacts the content.

questions.q: In the passage where the ten-day-old infant speaks ("O wise prophets!"), identify the grammatical mood of the verbs and explain how this impossible speech act functions as verbal irony.
questions.a: The verbs are in the indicative mood ("It was I who spoke," "I who spoke"), stating facts, but the content — a newborn articulating complex philosophical rebuttals — is biologically impossible, creating verbal irony: the literal meaning contradicts reality. A wrong answer (e.g., "it's magical realism") reveals the student confuses genre with rhetorical device; the irony targets astrological pretension, not fantasy.

questions.q: Compare the language register of the Maharaja's dialogue ("Let tigers beware!", "I can organise any other hunt...") with the British officer's secretary's reported request. What does the contrast reveal about power dynamics?
questions.a: The Maharaja uses imperative mood and declarative sentences with absolute certainty ("That's impossible!"), projecting sovereign command; the secretary's request is mediated, hedged ("the durai himself did not have to kill... What was important... was a photograph"), revealing the British officer's performative power vs. the Maharaja's substantive but fragile authority. A wrong answer (e.g., "both are powerful") misses how register encodes political tension — the Maharaja's blunt syntax resists colonial condescension.

questions.q: Evaluate the effectiveness of the final sentence — "In this manner the hundredth tiger took its final revenge upon the Tiger King" — as a closure to the story's grammatical pattern of ironic inversion.
questions.a: The sentence is highly effective: it inverts subject-object agency (the dead wooden tiger becomes the active agent "took revenge"), mirrors the opening's mock-epic register ("Tiger King" title), and completes the syntactic irony where every prediction (astrologer's, Maharaja's vow) is grammatically fulfilled but semantically subverted. A weak evaluation (e.g., "it's a good ending") shows the student cannot connect micro-level grammar to macro-level structural irony.

questions.q: Rewrite the dewan's dialogue ("Your Majesty! I am not a tiger!") as a formal reported speech sentence, then explain how the shift from direct to reported speech changes the comedic effect.
questions.a: Reported version: "The dewan exclaimed in terror that he was not a tiger." The shift flattens the comedy: direct speech preserves the dewan's panic-induced literalism (he misunderstands "thirty tigers remain to be shot down by this gun of mine" as a threat to him), while reported speech distances the reader from his voice, losing the timing and absurdity. A poor rewrite (e.g., "The dewan said he wasn't a tiger") misses how punctuation and verb choice ("exclaimed" vs "said") modulate tone.
